## Overview and grading

### What you'll practice

In this graded assignment, you will first do the following **without** genAI:
write a shell script to run the program TrimGalore, run it, and interpret its output.
Then, you'll use **Claude Code** to review and extend your script,
to write a loop that runs it for multiple samples,
and to summarize the results.

- **Deadline**: [Sunday Oct 25^th^ at 11:59 pm]{style="background-color: #faf678;"}.
- **Submission**: Like for GA3, you will submit your assignment by tagging the
  instructors in an Issue in your GitHub repository, as per the last step below.

### GenAI expectations

This is the first assignment in which you are allowed to use generative AI.
The general guidelines from now on are:

- You can use genAI as long as you **can explain what your code does**.
  If genAI produces commands or constructs not covered in class,
  do the research needed to understand them.
- Whatever the source, you remain responsible for whether the code is correct.

That said, this assignment has two exceptions to these guidelines:

- You must do **Part B without** genAI assistance (same rules as GA1–GA3).
  This is because in Part C, you'll compare genAI output with
  a script and answers you produced yourself.
- In **Part C**, genAI use is not just allowed but _required_:
  you must use Claude Code specifically (not another genAI tool),
  and document how you used it (item 17).
:::

You can earn a maximum of **0.5 points** for each of the 20 numbered

and 0 points for missing or incorrect answers).

### Part B: A TrimGalore script --- without genAI

TrimGalore [@krueger2026] is a commonly used tool to preprocess the reads
in FASTQ files before further analysis.
It's the next step in the RNA-seq analysis workflow we're gradually applying to
the @garrigós2025 data in this course:

![](/img/rnaseq-wf-3.png){fig-align="center" width="60%" fig-alt="A diagram showing the steps in an RNA-seq analysis pipeline." .lightbox}

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

TrimGalore takes FASTQ files as input,
and outputs filtered FASTQ files, along the way removing:

- Any adapter sequences that are present in the reads^[
  Adapters are always added to DNA/cDNA fragments of interest prior to Illumina sequencing,
  and the last bases of a read can "read through" into the adapter if the fragment
  is shorter than the read length.]
- Poor-quality bases at the end of the reads
- Reads that have become very short after the prior two steps

Unlike FastQC, TrimGalore isn't run on one FASTQ file at a time:
when you have paired-end reads, like we do with the @garrigós2025 data,
a **single** TrimGalore run should include **both** the R1 (forward read) and
R2 (reverse read) file for one sample.
This is because R1 and R2 files should remain "synced":
generally, you can't remove a read from an R1 file without also removing
its mate from the R2 file.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### More about TrimGalore and similar programs _(Click to expand)_

Several largely equivalent tools exist for this kind of FASTQ preprocessing ---
[Trimmomatic](http://www.usadellab.org/cms/index.php?page=trimmomatic) and
[fastp](https://github.com/OpenGene/fastp) are two other commonly used ones.
TrimGalore started out as a "wrapper" around yet another tool called Cutadapt,
but since version 2 (which we're using), it is a standalone program.
Two advantages of TrimGalore are:

- It will auto-detect the adapters that are present in your reads.
- It can automatically run FastQC on the trimmed sequences.
:::

03. Get a link from the Seqera Containers website to a **container** with
    TrimGalore version 2.3.0 (note: the package is called `trim-galore`).
    Then, print TrimGalore's help info by running `trim_galore --help` with your
    container link. Use this help info to find the TrimGalore options to:
    - Tell it that your reads are **paired-end**^[
      If you don't do this, TrimGalore will process the two FASTQ files independently.]
    - Set the **output dir**
    - Make it **run FastQC** on the trimmed FASTQ files

04. Also use the help info to find the **default thresholds** for
    A\) the base quality score and B\) the read length, and report what they are.
    _(You don't have to change these thresholds, the defaults work fine for us.)_

05. **Write a shell script** `scripts/trimgalore.sh` that runs TrimGalore
    on the R1 and R2 FASTQ files of **one** sample:
    - The script should accept three arguments:
      the R1 FASTQ file, the R2 FASTQ file, and the output dir.
    - Use the three options from question 3.
    - Include "logging statements" with `echo`, like in the FastQC script from class.
      (You don't need to separately print the TrimGalore version,
      since it is printed automatically when you run the program.)

    ::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
    #### Stick to using the default setting for the number of cores, for now. _(Click to expand)_
    Since you're running the program interactively on your single-core VS Code
    compute job, you only have 1 core at your disposal.
    Using 1 core is TrimGalore's default,
    so don't adjust this setting here with TrimGalore's `--cores` option.
    Next week, you'll learn to submit scripts as batch jobs,
    which gives you the opportunity to use multiple cores to speed things up.
    :::

06. **Run your script** for the FASTQ files of sample `S63` (in `../garrigos/fastq`),
    with `results/trimgalore` as the output dir.
    Then, list the files in the output dir,
    and briefly **describe** what each type of output file contains.
    Once your script works, commit it.
    (If it failed, try to fix your script,
    and briefly describe the problem and your fix in the README.)

07. TrimGalore printed quite a bit of logging output to the screen,
    while additional information is saved in the `*_trimming_report.txt` output files.
    Use this information to answer the following:
    - Which [adapter](../week01/w1b_omics-data.html#/a-closer-look-at-the-processed-dna-fragments)
      sequence did TrimGalore look for in the reads,
      and how did it decide on this (you didn't tell it which adapter to look for)?
    - In each file (R1 and R2), in what percentage of reads were adapters detected?
    - In each file, were more bases removed as a result of quality trimming or adapter trimming?
    - What percentage of read pairs were removed altogether?

08. TrimGalore also reports on **poly-G trimming**.
    Newer Illumina sequencers, such as the NextSeq and NovaSeq,
    use a "two-color" chemistry in which `G` bases produce no signal.
    As a result, when the signal is lost near the end of a read,
    the sequencer calls a stretch of false `G`s,
    which should be trimmed off.
    Use TrimGalore's logging output and the trimming reports to answer the following:
    - Did TrimGalore do poly-G trimming, and did you have to tell it to?
    - What does TrimGalore conclude about the sequencing technology
      that was used to generate these reads?
    - Was more poly-G trimming done in the R1 or the R2 file?
      _(Optional: any idea why?)_

09. Compare TrimGalore's FastQC report for the **trimmed** R1 file with the FastQC
    report for the **raw** R1 file of the same sample (the one you copied to `results/fastqc`).
    - Name at least two differences between the reports.
      Do things look better now in terms of pass/warn/fail status?
    - Do the short reads with only `N`s,
      which you saw [in week 4](/week04/w4c_shell-files2.qmd#less-to-page-through-files),
      appear to have been removed?
      If so, was that due to the length threshold, or something else?
    - Name something you didn't expect or are confused about.

    <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} To see the two files side by side, download one or both _(Click to expand)_</summary>

    The HTML preview in VS Code won't let you preview each file in a separate tab.
    So, to view them side by side, you can download one or both of the FastQC reports:
    in the file explorer, right-click on a file and click "Download...".
    Then, open the downloaded file(s) in your browser.

    </details>

### Part B: A TrimGalore script --- without genAI

<details><summary>**3.** A TrimGalore container, its help info, and three options</summary>

The container link (URI) for TrimGalore version 2.3.0 is:

```bash-in-nocolor
oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/trim-galore:2.3.0--a56e49e832976df4
```

Make sure to use the `oras://` URI rather than the Docker one.

To print the help info:

```bash
apptainer exec oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/trim-galore:2.3.0--a56e49e832976df4 \
    trim_galore --help
```

The relevant parts of the output:

```bash-out-solo
 USAGE:
Usage: trim_galore [OPTIONS] <INPUT>...

Arguments:
  <INPUT>...
          Input FASTQ file(s). For paired-end, provide two files

Options:

  --paired
        Paired-end mode. Accepts an even number of input files as consecutive
        R1/R2 pairs (e.g. --paired R1.fq.gz R2.fq.gz, or a glob matching multiple samples)

  -o, --output_dir <OUTPUT_DIR>
        Output directory for trimmed files. Created if it doesn't exist

  --fastqc
        Run FastQC on the trimmed output files
        (built in via the bundled fastqc-rust library; no external Java or FastQC binary needed).
        Produces FastQC 0.12.1-compatible *_fastqc.html / *_fastqc.zip artifacts
```

- `--paired` to indicate that the FASTQ files are paired-end
- `--output_dir` (or equivalently, `-o`) to specify the output dir
- `--fastqc` to run FastQC on the trimmed FASTQ files

</details>

<details><summary>**4.** Default thresholds</summary>

The relevant parts of the help output:

```bash-out-solo
  -q, --quality <QUALITY>
        Quality trimming cutoff (Phred score). Bases below this are trimmed from 3' end
        [default: 20]

      --length <LENGTH>
        Minimum required sequence length after trimming. Default: 20 (18 for smallRNA adapter).
        In paired-end mode, both reads must pass; see --retain_unpaired to keep single survivors
```

- A\) The default base quality score threshold (option `-q`/`--quality`) is **20**,
  which corresponds to an estimated 0.01 error rate.
  TrimGalore will trim bases with a lower quality score than this threshold
  from the **end** (3' end) of the reads ---
  it will **not** remove or mask low-quality bases elsewhere in the read,
  such as in the middle.

- B\) The default read length threshold (option `--length`) is **20 bp**:
  any reads that are shorter than this after adapter and quality trimming will be removed.
  With paired-end input, the corresponding other read will also be removed,
  regardless of its length:
  paired-end FASTQ files always need to contain both the R1 and R2 for each pair.

</details>

<details><summary>**5.** Write the `trimgalore.sh` script</summary>

```{.bash .file filename="scripts/trimgalore.sh"}
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Run TrimGalore on the paired-end FASTQ files of one sample
# Usage: bash scripts/trimgalore.sh <R1 FASTQ file> <R2 FASTQ file> <output dir>

# Constants
TRIMGALORE_CONTAINER=oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/trim-galore:2.3.0--a56e49e832976df4

# Copy the placeholder variables
fastq_r1="$1"
fastq_r2="$2"
outdir="$3"

# Initial logging
echo "Starting script trimgalore.sh"
date
echo "Input R1 FASTQ file:      $fastq_r1"
echo "Input R2 FASTQ file:      $fastq_r2"
echo "Output dir:               $outdir"
echo

# Create the output dir if needed
mkdir -p "$outdir"

# Run TrimGalore
apptainer exec "$TRIMGALORE_CONTAINER" \
    trim_galore \
    --paired \
    --fastqc \
    --output_dir "$outdir" \
    "$fastq_r1" \
    "$fastq_r2"

# Final logging
echo
echo "Successfully finished script trimgalore.sh"
date
```

- Using the container link directly in the `apptainer exec` commands,
  rather than storing it in a "constant" variable, is fine too.
- Since TrimGalore creates the output dir if it doesn't exist,
  the `mkdir -p` line isn't strictly necessary here,
  but it doesn't hurt either.

</details>

For each of the two input files, there are five output files:

- `*_val_*.fq.gz`: the trimmed FASTQ file
- `*_trimming_report.txt`: a text report of the trimming results
- `*_trimming_report.json`: the same kind of information,
  in a format that is easy for other programs to read (e.g. MultiQC)
- `*_fastqc.html` and `*_fastqc.zip`: the FastQC results for the trimmed FASTQ file

<details><summary>**7.** Trimming results</summary>

- **Adapters**: TrimGalore looked for the standard Illumina adapter (`AGATCGGAAGAGC`).
  You didn't tell it which adapter to look for: it auto-detected this,
  by counting how often each of several common adapter sequences occurred in the reads
  (the Illumina adapter was the best hit, and Nextera the second-best).
- **13.0%** (R1) and **10.1%** (R2) of reads had adapters.
- **Quality vs. adapter trimming**: in both files, more bases were removed by
  **quality trimming** (far more in R1).
  The "Summary" section of each trimming report lists the quality-trimmed bases directly,
  first for R1 and then for R2:

  ```bash-out-solo
  Total basepairs processed:     35,498,138 bp
  Quality-trimmed:                1,274,150 bp (3.6%)
  Total written (filtered):      34,138,461 bp (96.2%)
  ```

  ```bash-out-solo
  Total basepairs processed:     36,784,563 bp
  Quality-trimmed:                1,283,793 bp (3.5%)
  Total written (filtered):      35,440,230 bp (96.3%)
  ```

  The adapter-trimmed bases aren't listed directly,
  but they make up the rest of the difference between "processed" and "written":
  for R1, 35,498,138 − 1,274,150 − 34,138,461 = **85,527 bp** (0.24%),
  and for R2, **60,540 bp** (0.16%).
  Alternatively, the "Overview of removed sequences" table in each report shows that
  most adapter matches are only 1--3 bp long:
  for example, 54,817 of the 65,070 R1 reads with adapters had just 1 base removed.
  (The `expect` column shows that 125,000 such 1-bp matches would be expected by chance alone,
  so many of these "adapters" are probably just a read ending in an `A`.)

- **7.4%** of read pairs (37,016 of 500,000) were removed altogether:
  see the "Paired-end validation" section of the logging output,
  or of the R2 trimming report:

  ```bash-out-solo
  Number of sequence pairs removed because at least one read was shorter than the length cutoff (7.40%):
                                   37,016
  ```

</details>

<details><summary>**8.** Poly-G trimming</summary>

- TrimGalore **did** do poly-G trimming, and you didn't have to tell it to:
  "Poly-G trimming: ENABLED (auto-detected)".
- It concludes that the reads were likely generated with
  **two-color chemistry** (NovaSeq or NextSeq),
  since 0.23% of reads have poly-G tails of 10 bp or more.
- Much more poly-G trimming was done in the **R2** file:
  8.7% of reads and ~1.19 million bases, versus 2.4% of reads and ~90,000 bases in R1.
  _Optional_: R2 reads are sequenced after the R1 reads,
  by which time the clusters on the flow cell give a weaker signal ---
  just like you typically see lower quality scores in R2 files.

</details>

<details><summary>**9.** Compare the FastQC reports before and after trimming</summary>

There are clear differences in, for example:

- **Pass/warn/fail** status:
  "Per base N content" went from warn to pass,
  and "Overrepresented sequences" from fail to pass.
  Other modules kept their status, including "Per sequence GC content" (still fail).
- **Basic statistics**: the number of reads went from 500,000 to 462,984
  (500,000 minus the 37,016 removed pairs from question 7),
  and the read length range from 35--74 to 20--74 bp.
- The "Per sequence GC content", "Sequence Length Distribution",
  and "Overrepresented sequences" graphs,
  all of which had artefacts related to the very short reads that only
  contained `N`s: these reads have been removed by the trimming process.

Even reads like the 35-bp example from week 4 were removed,
even though they're longer than the 20-bp length threshold:
all of their bases had quality score `#` (Phred score 2),
so quality trimming removed every base.
The resulting empty (0 bp) reads were then removed by the length filter,
together with their mates.

There is no single correct answer to the last part.
For example, you might have been surprised that some modules still fail:
"Per base sequence content" commonly fails for RNA-seq data
because of biases in the first bases of the reads,
which trimming doesn't (and shouldn't) fix.

</details>

<details><summary>**14.** Claude writes a loop</summary>

A correct loop:

```bash
for fastq_r1 in ../garrigos/fastq/S6*_R1.fastq.gz; do
    fastq_r2="${fastq_r1/_R1/_R2}"
    bash scripts/trimgalore.sh "$fastq_r1" "$fastq_r2" results/trimgalore
done
```

- It loops over R1 files only, so it runs the script once per sample.
- It gets the R2 file name by replacing `_R1` with `_R2`.
  Because the search pattern includes the underscore,
  it doesn't have the `S61` pitfall from the w7b self-study:
  the `1` in a sample ID like `S61` is not preceded by `_R`.
- The `S6*` glob matches only the 7 samples `S63` to `S69`.
- Other correct approaches are fine too,
  such as looping over a list of sample IDs.

</details>
